client: I've been really struggling ever since my grandmother passed away six months ago. Family get-togethers used to feel warm and comfortable, but now when I'm around my relatives, I just feel... hollow, like I'm watching everyone from behind glass. I'm not even sure talking about it will change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and being here — even when part of you doubts it will help, showing up takes real courage. The way you describe feeling hollow and disconnected at family gatherings makes a lot of sense; grief can quietly reshape the spaces that once felt safe, leaving us feeling like outsiders in our own lives. What you're experiencing sounds like a painful mix of loss and longing, and I'd really like to gently explore together what thoughts and meanings are showing up for you in those moments.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess the main thought that keeps coming up is that I should be handling this better by now — six months feels like it should be enough time to start feeling normal again, but I still can't get through a family dinner without wanting to slip away early. And there's this guilt too, like everyone else seems to be moving on and I'm just... stuck, which makes me feel even more isolated because I don't want to bring the mood down by talking about her. It's hard to explain without feeling like I'm being dramatic.
therapist: That thought — "I should be over this by now" — is one of the most common and quietly painful things grief does to us, and it's worth gently challenging: who actually set that timeline, and where did it come from? The way you're speaking, softly and carefully, tells me you're carrying something heavy while also trying very hard not to take up too much space, which mirrors exactly what you're describing — shrinking yourself at dinners to protect others from your grief. You're not being dramatic; you're describing a very real burden of mourning alone while surrounded by people you love.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I never really thought about where that timeline came from — I think I just absorbed it somehow, maybe from seeing other people seem okay after a few months, or just this general sense that grief has an expiration date. But even knowing that the timeline might be made up doesn't automatically make the feeling go away, you know? I still sit at those dinners and feel this pressure to act normal, and I'm not sure just recognizing the thought will be enough to change how I actually feel in those moments.
therapist: You're making a really important distinction — insight alone doesn't automatically rewire how we *feel* in the moment, and you're right to name that. Your voice carries something that sounds like quiet exhaustion, like you've been holding this tension carefully for a long time, and that fast, soft way of speaking suggests you might be working hard to get the words out before the feeling catches up with you. In CBT, we'd work not just on recognizing the thought but on building small, concrete ways to respond differently *in* those moments — so I'm curious, when you feel that pressure to act normal at dinner, what does "acting normal" actually cost you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, it costs me a lot of energy — I spend the whole dinner monitoring myself, making sure I laugh at the right moments and don't let my face go blank when someone mentions her casually, like she's just a fond memory instead of this huge absence. By the time I get home I'm completely drained, and then I feel guilty for being drained because I should want to be around my family. I guess I never framed it as a cost before, it just felt like what I had to do to get through it.
therapist: What you just described — that constant, exhausting performance of "okay-ness" — is actually a really significant thing to name, and I notice even the way you're speaking, softly and with a kind of careful steadiness, reflects that same effortful containment you're describing at those dinners. That guilt for being drained is another layer of the same pattern: you're not allowed to grieve *and* you're not allowed to be tired from hiding your grief, which is an incredibly unfair double bind your mind has constructed. What if being drained wasn't a sign of weakness, but simply honest evidence of how much she still matters to you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That reframe is... actually kind of nice to hear, and part of me wants to hold onto it. But I'm worried that in the moment, when I'm sitting at the table and my aunt makes a joke about something grandma used to do, I won't be able to access that thought — it'll just feel like a nice thing someone said in a therapy office that doesn't survive contact with real life. How do you actually make something like that stick when your emotions are moving faster than your thoughts?
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — quick, a little breathless, pitched higher — tells me this question feels urgent and real, like you're already anticipating that moment at the table and bracing for it. You're asking exactly the right thing, and you're right that insight doesn't survive high-emotion moments on its own, which is why in CBT we practice building what are called "anchors" — small, physical or behavioral micro-responses you rehearse *before* the moment, so they become automatic rather than something you have to think your way to. It might be something as simple as a breath, a phrase, or even a quiet permission you give yourself — and I'd love to work with you on finding one that feels like *yours*, not just something borrowed from a therapy office.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I like the idea of it feeling like mine, because you're right that borrowed things tend to slide off when I'm actually in it. I'm trying to think of what that anchor might even be, and the honest answer is I'm drawing a blank — I'm not sure I know myself well enough in those moments to know what would actually help. Maybe that's part of the problem, that I've been so focused on suppressing everything that I don't even know what I actually need anymore.
therapist: What you just said — "I don't even know what I need anymore" — is actually one of the most honest and courageous things you could recognize, and your voice carries something that sounds like a quiet, genuine searching rather than defeat. The years of suppressing your grief to protect others may have genuinely dimmed your access to your own inner signals, and that's not a personal failing — it's what happens when we spend too long being a caretaker of everyone else's comfort. So rather than trying to find the anchor right now, I wonder if we could start somewhere smaller: in those dinner moments, before the performance kicks in, is there even a brief flicker of something — a feeling, a sensation, an impulse — that you've been trained to immediately push down?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, actually — there's this moment right when I sit down at the table where I have this impulse to say her name, just to acknowledge that she's not there, that there's this empty chair. But I shut it down almost instantly because I can picture everyone's faces getting uncomfortable, and I don't want to be the one who makes the dinner heavy. I think I've been so fast at pushing that down that I almost forgot it was even happening until you just asked.
therapist: The fact that you're speaking so quickly right now, like the words are tumbling out before you can stop them, tells me that rediscovering that impulse feels both significant and a little startling — as if you've just found something you didn't realize you'd lost. That moment you described, the urge to say her name, isn't you trying to make dinner heavy; it's actually a profound act of love, a refusal to let her disappear into comfortable silence. I wonder what it would mean to you — not to everyone else, but just to *you* — if that impulse were allowed to exist, even privately, as a small internal acknowledgment rather than something that has to be immediately extinguished.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: If I let that impulse just exist privately, even for a second, I think it might actually crack something open — and I'm not sure I'm ready for that, especially not at a dinner table surrounded by people. There's something almost protective about shutting it down so fast, like if I don't let myself feel it fully, I can keep functioning. But I also hear what you're saying, and some part of me is tired of protecting everyone else from something they probably feel too and are just as busy hiding.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, with something almost fragile in your voice — tells me that last thought, that everyone else might be hiding the same thing, landed somewhere deep and real for you. You've named something really important: that the protection you've been offering your family may actually be a wall that's keeping everyone alone in their grief together, which is a quietly heartbreaking kind of loneliness. You don't have to crack everything open at once — but I wonder if the exhaustion you're feeling isn't just from hiding your grief, but from carrying the weight of a silence that was never really yours to carry alone.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That framing hits harder than I expected — the idea that I've been carrying a silence that wasn't mine to carry alone makes me feel both relieved and a little angry, like I've been doing this unnecessary job for six months without realizing it. But then I immediately wonder, what if I'm wrong and my family actually is okay and I'm the only one still stuck here, and bringing it up would just make me look like I can't move on. I don't know how you'd even test something like that without risking making everything awkward or worse.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, pitched high, like something urgent is pressing through — tells me that anger and relief are both real and alive in you simultaneously, and that's not confusion, that's actually a really healthy sign that something true is breaking through. That fear of being wrong, of being "the only one still stuck," is worth examining gently — because notice that your mind immediately used it to pull you back from the relief, which is a pattern worth paying attention to. Testing whether your family shares this grief doesn't have to mean a dramatic announcement at dinner; it might start as something much smaller, like letting one trusted person in, and we could think together about what that might look like.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: There is one person I keep almost reaching out to — my cousin, who was really close with grandma too, and sometimes I catch her going quiet at dinners in the same way I do. But even thinking about texting her feels scary, because what if I open something up between us and then neither of us knows how to close it, and it just makes things harder instead of better. I guess I'm afraid that letting one person in means I can't keep pretending everything is fine, and I'm not sure I'm ready to give up that pretending even though I know it's costing me.
therapist: The way you're speaking right now — very fast, pitched high, with something almost urgent pressing through — suggests that even describing the possibility of reaching out to your cousin is activating something significant, like part of you is already halfway there and frightening yourself with it. What you just named so honestly is the real cost of the pretending: it's not just exhausting, it's actually standing between you and the one person who might already be sitting in the same silence, catching your eye across the same dinner table. That fear of opening something you can't close is worth sitting with — but I'd gently offer that what you're describing doesn't sound like a door that would break things, but one that might finally let some air in for both of you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
